rows.stem: A woman having genes for haemophilia on one X chromosome and a gene for colour blindness on another X chromosome marries a normal man. The progeny will show

options.label: A
options.text: 50% haemophilic and colour-blind sons, 50% normal sons.

options.label: B
options.text: 50% haemophilic carrier daughter, 50% colour-blind carrier daughters.

options.label: C
options.text: All sons and daughters colour-blind and haemophilic.

options.label: D
options.text: Only haemophilic and colour-blind daughters.

rows.solution:
Haemophilia and colour blindness are both **sex-linked recessive** traits carried on the X chromosome. The woman carries the haemophilia allele on one X and the colour blindness allele on the other, so she is \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\text{X}^{\text{c}}\); the normal man is \(\text{X}\text{Y}\).
- Daughters receive the father's normal X and one X from the mother: half are \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\text{X}\) (**carriers of haemophilia**) and half are \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\text{X}\) (**carriers of colour blindness**). The normal X from the father masks the recessive allele, so no daughter is affected.
- Sons receive the Y from the father and one X from the mother: half are \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\text{Y}\) (haemophilic) and half are \(\text{X}^{\text{c}}\text{Y}\) (colour-blind). No son is normal, and no son has both disorders, since the two alleles sit on different X chromosomes.

So the answer is option (B) 50% haemophilic carrier daughter, 50% colour-blind carrier daughters.

rows.stem: Which of the following is an important parameter for assessing the impact of any biotic or abiotic factor on population growth ?

options.label: A
options.text: Birth rate

options.label: B
options.text: K-carrying capacity

options.label: C
options.text: Death rate

options.label: D
options.text: r-Intrinsic rate of natural increase

rows.solution: In exponential growth the rate of increase of a population is \(\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\), where r is the **intrinsic rate of natural increase** (birth rate minus death rate per individual). Because r sums up the combined effect of births and deaths, NCERT describes it as a very important parameter chosen for assessing the impact of any biotic or abiotic factor on population growth. Birth rate or death rate alone captures only half the picture, and the carrying capacity K is the ceiling the environment sets, not a rate. So the answer is option (D) r-Intrinsic rate of natural increase.

rows.stem: If a sperm nucleus is injected into an oocyte then all of the following events are bypassed except -

options.label: A
options.text: The swimming of sperm to meet the egg in the oviduct.

options.label: B
options.text: The sperm's acquisition of motility in the epididymis.

options.label: C
options.text: A sperm comes in contact with the zona pellucida layer of the ovum.

options.label: D
options.text: The complex process like cell division and cell differentiation.

rows.stem: If A = species richness and B = Endemism then biodiversity hotspots have

options.label: A
options.text: low degree of A and low degree of B.

options.label: B
options.text: low degree of A and high degree of B.

options.label: C
options.text: high degree of A and low degree of B.

options.label: D
options.text: high degree of A and high degree of B.

rows.solution: **Biodiversity hotspots** are regions with very high levels of species richness and a high degree of **endemism**, that is, species confined to that region and found nowhere else. These are the two criteria used to identify them, and the hotspots are given priority in in situ conservation because they are also regions of accelerated habitat loss. So the answer is option (D) high degree of A and high degree of B.

rows.stem: Two plants whose DNA has been sequenced are

options.label: A
options.text: Rice and Wheat

options.label: B
options.text: Wheat and Maize

options.label: C
options.text: Maize and Barley

options.label: D
options.text: Rice and Arabidopsis

rows.solution: After the Human Genome Project, the genomes of several non-human model organisms were also sequenced: bacteria, yeast, Caenorhabditis elegans (a free-living non-pathogenic nematode), Drosophila (the fruit fly), and the plants **rice and Arabidopsis**. So the answer is option (D) Rice and Arabidopsis.

rows.stem: Antivenom injection is an example of

options.label: A
options.text: Natural Active Immunity

options.label: B
options.text: Artificial Active Immunity

options.label: C
options.text: Natural Passive Immunity

options.label: D
options.text: Artificial Passive Immunity

rows.solution: In snakebite the venom acts too fast for the body to make its own antibodies in time, so the patient is injected with **preformed antibodies** (antitoxin) against the venom. When ready-made antibodies are given directly to the body, the immunity is **passive**, and because they are given by injection rather than received naturally (as a foetus receives them through the placenta or a baby through colostrum), it is **artificial**. So the answer is option (D) Artificial Passive Immunity.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Pollen grains have a mucilaginous covering on them in most of the water pollinating plants.
Reason (R) : Mucilaginous covering help pollen grains to be submerged in water.
rows.context: For Question numbers 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from Code (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation for Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not correct explanation for Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: in most of the water-pollinated species, the pollen grains carry a **mucilaginous covering**. The Reason is false: the covering does not help the pollen to submerge, it **protects the pollen grains from wetting**. Many water-pollinated plants in fact carry the pollen on or near the water surface, as in Vallisneria, where the released pollen grains are carried passively by water currents to the stigma. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.stem:
Is it possible for a trait to be inherited by an organism but not expressed in its phenotype ?
Justify and illustrate your answer with a suitable Mendelian Cross.
rows.solution:
**Yes.** A trait can be inherited by an organism and still not appear in its phenotype, when its allele is **recessive** and is masked by a dominant allele in the heterozygote. Mendel's monohybrid cross on height in garden pea shows this.

Parents: tall (TT) \(\times\) dwarf (tt). Gametes: T from the tall parent, t from the dwarf parent.

\(\text{F}_1\): all Tt, all **tall**. The dwarf allele t is present but not expressed.

\(\text{F}_1 \times \text{F}_1\): Tt \(\times\) Tt, gametes T and t from each.

| | T | t |
|---|---|---|
| T | TT, tall | Tt, tall |
| t | Tt, tall | tt, dwarf |

\(\text{F}_2\): 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

The dwarf trait is not expressed in the \(\text{F}_1\) generation but **reappears in the \(\text{F}_2\)** generation. So it was inherited by the \(\text{F}_1\) plants all along, without being expressed in their phenotype. The same reasoning works with any other pair of contrasting traits.

rows.stem: Explain the two major approaches used while sequencing the total DNA from a cell.
rows.solution:
The two major approaches used in sequencing the total DNA of a cell (as in the Human Genome Project) are:
- **Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs)**: this approach focuses on identifying all the genes that are **expressed as RNA**.
- **Sequence Annotation**: the **blind approach** of simply sequencing the whole set of the genome, which contains all the coding and non-coding sequences, and later assigning different regions in the sequence with functions.

rows.subtopic: Isolation, Cutting and Amplification of DNA
rows.stem: Briefly describe the process of DNA extraction from a fungal cell. Name the chemicals used in the process.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: it says chitinase digests the "membrane"; chitin is the material of the fungal cell **wall**, and chitinase breaks the wall, as NCERT states.] DNA is enclosed within the cell along with other macromolecules, so it has to be released and purified:
- The fungal cell is treated with the enzyme **chitinase**, which breaks the chitin cell wall and releases the DNA along with RNA, proteins, polysaccharides and lipids.
- RNA is removed by treatment with **ribonuclease**.
- Proteins are removed by treatment with **protease**.
- Other molecules are removed by appropriate treatments, and **chilled ethanol** is then added, which makes the purified DNA precipitate out as a mass of fine threads.

Chemicals used: chitinase, ribonuclease, protease and chilled ethanol.

rows.stem:
Differentiate between opioids and cannabinoids on the basis of their
(a) Receptor site in human body.
(b) Mode of action in human body.
rows.solution:
| Basis | Opioids | Cannabinoids |
|---|---|---|
| (a) Receptor site in human body | Specific opioid receptors in the **central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract** | Cannabinoid receptors present principally in the **brain** |
| (b) Mode of action in human body | A **depressant**: slows down body functions (heroin is the best known example) | Known for their effects on the **cardiovascular system** of the body |

rows.stem: Chasmogamous flowers remain open and expose their reproductive parts. Explain how this structural feature supports different types of pollination.
rows.solution:
Chasmogamous flowers are **open flowers with exposed anthers and stigma**, similar to the flowers of other species. Because both the pollen and the receptive stigma are exposed, pollen can reach the stigma from several sources, so all three types of pollination become possible:
- **Autogamy**: pollen grains from the anther are transferred to the stigma of the **same flower**. In an open flower this needs the release of pollen and the receptivity of the stigma to be synchronised, and the anthers and stigma to lie close to each other.
- **Geitonogamy**: pollen grains are transferred from the anther of one flower to the stigma of **another flower of the same plant**, carried by an agent such as wind, water or animals.
- **Xenogamy**: pollen grains are transferred from the anther of one flower to the stigma of a flower on **a different plant**, which brings genetically different pollen to the stigma.

This is the difference from cleistogamous flowers, which never open, so their anthers and stigma stay enclosed and only autogamy is possible.

rows.stem:
(i) Identify the structure shown above and name the process taking place.
(ii) Write the source of energy for the process and list the enzymes involved.
(iii) Mention the difference in the process based on polarity. What terms are used for such synthesis ?
(iv) Redraw the structure after completion of the process and label the newly synthesised parts.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a line drawing printed before sub-part (i), with no lead sentence: two parallel vertical strands that separate at their lower end into two diverging arms, the two upper ends and the two lower ends each labelled 5' or 3'. The drawing is the only statement of the structure that (i) asks the student to identify, and its end labels decide the polarity that (iii) asks about, so the structure's name and which end carries which label are withheld here. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: its list of enzymes includes permease, which is the transport protein of the lac operon (coded by the y gene) and takes no part in replication; the replication enzymes are DNA-dependent DNA polymerase, helicase, topoisomerase and DNA ligase.]

(i) The structure is a **replication fork**, the small opening where the two strands of the DNA double helix separate. The process taking place is **DNA replication**.

(ii) The source of energy is the **deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates** (dNTPs), which serve a dual purpose: they act as the substrates and also provide the energy for the polymerisation reaction. Enzymes involved: **DNA-dependent DNA polymerase** (main enzyme, joins nucleotides), **helicase** (unwinds the helix), **topoisomerase** (relieves the strain of unwinding) and **DNA ligase** (joins the discontinuous fragments).

(iii) DNA polymerase can polymerise nucleotides **only in the 5' to 3' direction**. So:
- on the template strand with polarity **3' to 5'**, the new strand is synthesised **continuously** (the leading strand);
- on the template strand with polarity **5' to 3'**, the new strand is synthesised **discontinuously** in short fragments, the Okazaki fragments, which are later joined by DNA ligase (the lagging strand).

The terms used for such synthesis are **continuous synthesis** and **discontinuous synthesis**.

(iv) The redrawn structure shows the fork with the two parental strands (labelled 5' and 3' at the top as printed) separating into two arms, each now paired with a newly synthesised strand drawn antiparallel to it:
- along the left arm, whose template runs 3' to 5' towards the fork, one unbroken new strand labelled **continuous synthesis**, with its 5' end at the open end of the arm and its 3' end towards the fork;
- along the right arm, whose template runs 5' to 3' towards the fork, a row of short new pieces labelled **discontinuous synthesis**, each running 5' to 3' away from the fork;
- both new strands labelled **newly synthesised strands**.

rows.stem:
(i) How would you find out whether a given tall garden pea plant is homozygous or heterozygous ?
Substantiate your answer with the help of Punnet square.
(ii) Given below are \(\text{F}_2\) phenotypic ratios of two independently carried monohybrid crosses.
(1) 1 : 2 : 1
(2) 3 : 1
Mention what does each ratio suggest.
rows.solution:
(i) Whether a tall pea plant is homozygous (TT) or heterozygous (Tt) cannot be told from its phenotype. It is found out by a **test cross**: the tall plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a **dwarf plant (tt), the homozygous recessive parent**, and the progeny are examined.

Case 1: the tall plant is homozygous. TT (dominant phenotype, genotype unknown) \(\times\) tt (homozygous recessive).

| | t | t |
|---|---|---|
| T | Tt | Tt |
| T | Tt | Tt |

Result: **all the progeny are tall**. Interpretation: the unknown plant is **homozygous (TT)**.

Case 2: the tall plant is heterozygous. Tt (dominant phenotype, genotype unknown) \(\times\) tt (homozygous recessive).

| | t | t |
|---|---|---|
| T | Tt | Tt |
| t | tt | tt |

Result: **50% of the progeny are tall and 50% are dwarf** (ratio 1 : 1). Interpretation: the unknown plant is **heterozygous (Tt)**.

(ii)
- (1) An \(\text{F}_2\) phenotypic ratio of **1 : 2 : 1** suggests **incomplete dominance**: the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype, so the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio, as in the red, pink and white flowers of dog flower (snapdragon).
- (2) An \(\text{F}_2\) phenotypic ratio of **3 : 1** suggests **complete dominance**: the dominant allele fully masks the recessive one in the heterozygote, as in Mendel's tall and dwarf pea plants.
